Chapter 16INPUT

The Endless Stair

Everyone agrees there is a beach at the bottom.

At the far western edge of the city a long wooden staircase drops through the trees toward Wreck Beach. Everyone agrees there is a beautiful beach at the bottom. Nobody agrees on how many steps it takes to get there. The stair is the city's way out. It feeds something Terminal City cannot make for itself: scale, sky, sea, the feeling of leaving the useful world behind for a while. People stand at the bottom and feel small and glad about it, and the city receives that too. The stairs know when you are counting. Stop, and they add steps.

On the third morning, the Kid leaves Trout Lake carrying a skateboard and no paint. At the courtyard the others are looking at sketches. There will still be a wall in the afternoon.

After the bus ride west, the Kid stands at the top of the wooden stairs above Wreck Beach. Trees hide the bottom. The board goes under one arm. The descent begins with a count kept under the breath.

Halfway down, light opens between the trunks. The Kid stops counting to look. Below the next landing, there seem to be more steps than there were a moment ago. The Kid sighs and begins the count again. After three steps, the sea flashes between the trees. The Kid looks at it, looks at the next flight, and gives up counting.

The Endless Stair is one of the city's ways out of being useful for a while. At the bottom are sea, sky and enough distance to make a wall feel small. People come down for that without needing another reason. The stairs can keep their own accounting.

At the beach, the Kid sits on the board above the wet sand. In a shallow pool among the nearby stones, a small crab moves sideways through the reflected sky and disappears beneath a ledge. The Kid watches the water settle. On a scrap of paper, one line marks the horizon. Most of the page stays empty.

Later, back at the courtyard, the sketch is set beside the others. The Kid points to a gap between two painted branches. Nobody reaches to fill it. There is room enough to leave something open.

The ruleIf you stop counting, the staircase adds steps.

Terminal City is an original fictional mythology inspired by Vancouver’s geography, weather, wildlife, infrastructure, art, and electronic music. It makes no claim to historical, Indigenous, or religious tradition. Real places are used as settings; the operating system layered on them is invented.
Made by Steve Hiehn, a software developer and electronic musician based in Vancouver, Canada. All music was created using a custom DAW, Signals & Sorcery.
